title: NeuroQuest
subtitle:
The 3D Spatial Memory Palace
for Education
notes:
Good morning respected lecturers and fellow students. We are presenting NeuroQuest, a web application that gives study concepts a place inside a virtual memory palace. A student can attach a note to an object, return to its location, and try to remember the concept before opening the answer. Today we will explain the purpose, demonstrate the learning process, and describe how the website works. The current implementation runs in the browser and saves study data locally.
Source: README.md and src/components/NeuroQuest.tsx. Cover image is an AI-generated concept illustration, not a screenshot of the application.

title: The purpose of NeuroQuest
lead: Help students organize concepts in memorable places and practise recalling them before checking their notes.
items: A place for each idea
Connect a concept with an object and a location.
A reason to retrieve
Hide the answer during Recall Challenge.
A personal study space
Create subject palaces and track self-rated progress.
notes:
The main purpose is to support an active study habit. Students often have many notes, but need a practical way to return to a concept and check whether they can remember it. NeuroQuest combines a spatial cue with a recall prompt. The 3D object is the cue, the note contains the explanation, and the challenge asks the student to retrieve the idea before revealing it. The app supports revision. It does not replace explanation, problem solving, or a teacher's guidance.
Source: README.md; src/components/ui/AnchorDrawer.tsx.

title: The learning problem

columns.heading: Study challenges
items: Notes can become difficult to navigate.
Recognizing an answer can feel like remembering it.
Students need a simple way to revisit weak concepts.

columns.heading: Our design response
items: Separate subjects into named palaces.
Use location and artifact identity as cues.
Reveal answers after a recall attempt and record a rating.

foot: The project addresses a study workflow. Its effect on student marks has not been measured.
notes:
This slide explains the problem our design aims to address, rather than claiming that every student has the same difficulty. NeuroQuest offers a visual route through study material and a deliberate pause before viewing an answer. Research on retrieval practice motivates the recall step. However, we have not run a controlled educational study of this particular application, so we cannot claim a percentage improvement in memory or marks.
Source: project requirements; Roediger and Karpicke (2006), https://doi.org/10.1111/j.1467-9280.2006.01693.x.

title: The memory palace idea

columns.heading: Method of Loci
items: Associate information with distinct locations.
Use a familiar route to revisit those associations.
In NeuroQuest, a geometric artifact holds the note.

columns.heading: Active recall
items: Look at the location and attempt an answer.
Reveal the concept and compare.
Rate the attempt and revisit what was difficult.

foot: Research motivates these techniques. It does not establish NeuroQuest's educational effectiveness.
notes:
The Method of Loci links information to places. NeuroQuest provides a digital space where the student can form those associations. A crystal might represent one concept while a ring represents another. During recall, the title is hidden and the student tries to identify the idea from its place. Research on mnemonic training and retrieval practice supports the rationale for exploring this approach, but those studies did not test NeuroQuest.
Sources: Dresler et al. (2017), https://doi.org/10.1016/j.neuron.2017.02.003; Roediger and Karpicke (2006), https://doi.org/10.1111/j.1467-9280.2006.01693.x.

title: What the website includes
rows: Subject palaces
Computer Science, Human Anatomy, World History, and custom subjects.
Memory anchors
Notes linked to geometric artifacts, colors, and 3D positions.
Study tools
Explore, Recall Challenge, search, editing, and learning insights.
Accessible controls
Anchor lists and a map support the 3D view. An HTML fallback keeps study available.
notes:
NeuroQuest begins with three example subjects. The new Create palace feature allows students to add other subjects, such as Mathematics or Chemistry. Every palace has its own anchors. Each anchor contains a title, category, Markdown content, shape, color, and position. Students can find anchors through the scene, map, list, or search. The anatomical and historical subjects currently use geometric artifacts and notes, not detailed anatomical simulations or reconstructed historical locations.
Sources: src/lib/data.ts; src/lib/types.ts; src/components/NeuroQuest.tsx; src/components/ui/AddRoomModal.tsx.

title: How a student uses NeuroQuest
steps: Choose a subject
Open an existing palace or create a new one.
Add a concept
Write a focused note and select its artifact.
Explore the room
Learn the note and notice its location.
Try Recall Challenge
Attempt the answer before revealing it.
Rate and revisit
Choose Easy, Hard, or Failed and continue.
notes:
This is the full student workflow. Begin with one small topic and a few clear anchors. In Explore mode, read and understand the material. Then switch to Recall Challenge, select an object, and answer aloud or on paper before revealing the note. Rate the attempt honestly. Easy marks the anchor as mastered, while Hard and Failed mark it as learning. Students choose when to return. The current version does not automatically schedule spaced repetition.
Source: README.md, Explore and study and Recall challenge sections.

title: Creating a new subject palace
rows: Open the form
Select Create palace under Your palaces. On mobile, open the navigation menu.
Make it recognizable
Enter a unique name, an optional description, an icon, and a color.
Add the first memory
The empty palace opens immediately, ready for a new anchor.
Keep it for later
Rooms and notes remain in the same browser after refresh.
foot: Current limits: 50 palaces, names up to 48 characters, and 300 anchors across the workspace.
notes:
To demonstrate the feature, create a subject such as Mathematics. Choose an icon and a color that make it easy to recognize in the sidebar. The palace begins empty, so the next action is to add a memory anchor. Recall Challenge stays disabled until the room contains an anchor. Duplicate palace names are rejected. These limits are validation choices in the current implementation, rather than claims about the maximum capacity of the underlying technologies.
Sources: src/components/ui/AddRoomModal.tsx; src/store/usePalaceStore.ts; src/components/ui/ModeSwitcher.tsx.

title: Explore and Recall Challenge
foot: Ratings are self-assessments. The application does not automatically grade an answer.
notes:
These modes have different jobs. Explore mode supports learning the material and becoming familiar with the location. Recall Challenge removes the title cue and darkens the scene. After an attempt, the student reveals the concept and gives a rating. The app accepts one rating per anchor in a recall session. Changing the room or mode clears the session, but saved mastery and review counts remain.
Sources: src/components/ui/AnchorDrawer.tsx; src/components/three/Scene.tsx; src/store/usePalaceStore.ts.

title: Example: a Computer Science concept
label: BINARY TREES
lead: Place the concept at a distinctive location, then use that location as a recall cue.
items: Study note
A binary tree allows each node to have at most two children.
Recall prompt
What concept is anchored here? Explain the key idea before revealing it.
Follow-up practice
Draw a small tree and identify its root, leaves, and subtrees.
foot: Illustrative study activity. Understanding and worked examples still matter.
notes:
Imagine assigning Binary Trees to a memorable artifact near one corner of the room. First read the definition, draw an example, and connect the idea with that location. During Recall Challenge, identify the concept and explain it before revealing the note. A correct label alone is not the same as full understanding, so the student should also solve relevant exercises. The artifact is a memory cue. It is not a visual simulation of the data structure.
Source: project workflow in README.md; illustrative classroom example.

title: Value for students and lecturers

columns.heading: For students
items: A personal space for each subject.
A clear routine for practising recall.
Editable notes, categories, and code blocks.
Visible self-rated progress.

columns.heading: For lecturers
items: A visual way to demonstrate a revision method.
Concept-based activities for classroom discussion.
A project that connects education with web graphics.
A starting point for a supervised learning study.

foot: Lecturer dashboards, shared classes, and automatic grading are future possibilities.
notes:
The practical value is the study workflow and the ability to make subject-specific spaces. Students can use it for terminology, definitions, historical events, or programming concepts. Lecturers can demonstrate how to build associations and ask students to explain a concept after recalling it. This version does not provide a teacher account or class analytics. Those would require additional backend and permission features. The benefits listed here describe intended uses and implemented affordances, not measured improvements in grades.
Source: implemented features in README.md; proposed educational uses.

title: Languages and technologies
table: Application logic, typed data, and React components
Page structure, responsive layouts, and styling
Shared state and persistence on the device
Development tools, build process, and local serving
foot: Tailwind CSS, Drei, GSAP, Markdown libraries, and postprocessing support the experience.
notes:
TypeScript is the main programming language. TSX combines TypeScript with the component markup used by React. HTML describes the document structure and CSS controls its appearance. Next.js is a framework, React is a UI library, and Node.js is the runtime used for development and serving the build. Three.js handles the graphics, while React Three Fiber integrates that scene with React. JSON is a data format used for saved data and exports. There is no Python or Java backend in the website.
Source: package.json; src/lib/types.ts; src/app/globals.css.

title: Frontend architecture
table: Loads the application shell and client workspace
Navigation, search, settings, map, and progress
New rooms, notes, editing, recall, and ratings
Validates actions and connects the UI with the scene
Environment, anchors, camera, and visual effects
foot: WebGL loads only in the browser. Unsaved form input stays in component state.
notes:
The frontend separates responsibilities into modules. The App Router page mounts the NeuroQuest workspace. The workspace brings together study controls and a dynamically loaded scene. The scene has server rendering disabled because WebGL requires the browser. Components subscribe to specific parts of the Zustand store. Unsaved form inputs remain local to the form, so typing does not update the shared scene state on every keystroke. This separation makes the implementation easier to maintain.
Sources: src/app/page.tsx; src/components/NeuroQuest.tsx; src/store/usePalaceStore.ts.

title: How the 3D experience works
rows: Scene
Procedural architecture, lighting, a floor grid, and pedestals.
MemoryAnchor
Six artifact shapes with gentle hovering, rotation, and hover feedback.
CameraController
Bounded orbit controls and smooth focus transitions using GSAP.
PostProcessing
Bloom, vignette, and subtle chromatic aberration create atmosphere.
foot: Reduced-motion support, adjustable effects, and an HTML fallback support different devices.
notes:
Three.js renders the scene through WebGL. React Three Fiber manages declarative objects, and Drei provides useful controls and labels. Selecting an anchor updates a camera target. The camera controller moves to it smoothly, while bounded controls prevent extreme movement. Postprocessing adds a glow, with Bloom threshold 0.6 and intensity 1.2. Reduced-motion users receive immediate camera framing and no idle artifact movement. React Three Fiber disposes of declarative geometries and materials on unmount, and the camera controller cancels unused tweens.
Sources: src/components/three/Scene.tsx, MemoryAnchor.tsx, CameraController.tsx, PostProcessing.tsx.

title: Data and local persistence

columns.heading: Saved on this browser
items: Rooms and memory anchors.
Mastery status and review counts.
Latest review time and selected preferences.
Schema version 2 with older-data migration.

columns.heading: Important boundaries
items: No cross-device synchronization.
Clearing site data removes saved content.
JSON export is available.
An import screen and full review history are not included.

foot: Storage key: neuroquest-palace. localStorage is browser storage, not a backend database.
notes:
The app uses Zustand persistence to save selected state as JSON in localStorage. The saved data is validated when loaded. Version 1 data migrates to version 2, which includes custom rooms. Camera position and the current recall-session ratings are temporary. The stored latest review time and count are not a complete history of every answer. Export all palaces downloads a snapshot, but the app currently has no interface for importing that snapshot. Students should understand that their data belongs to this browser and origin.
Source: src/store/usePalaceStore.ts; exportPalace in src/components/NeuroQuest.tsx.

title: Backend: current scope and future plan

columns.heading: Current implementation
items: Next.js serves the built application.
Study logic runs in the browser.
No application API or server database.
No login, accounts, or shared classroom data.

columns.heading: Proposed extension
items: Authenticated API for rooms and anchors.
Database tables for users and review events.
Ownership checks and controlled sharing.
Backup, synchronization, and conflict handling.

foot: A future option is Next.js Route Handlers with PostgreSQL. This is a proposal, not implemented functionality.
notes:
It is important to distinguish the web server from an application backend. Node.js and Next.js serve this website, but the project does not currently have server-side study APIs, accounts, or a database. A future version could add authenticated Route Handlers and PostgreSQL tables. Every request would need server-side validation and ownership checks. Shared classroom features would also need role and permission design. We should present this as future development, not describe it as an existing backend.
Sources: project source inventory, package.json, README.md. Future architecture is a proposal.

steps: Model the learning data
Define rooms, anchors, modes, and retention types.
Build the workspace
Create navigation, note forms, drawers, and search.
Add the spatial scene
Connect artifacts and camera targets to shared state.
Implement recall and saving
Validate ratings, persist data, and migrate older records.
Verify and package
Run tests and checks, build, and serve the application.
foot: Local setup: npm ci, then npm run dev. Production: npm run build, then npm start.
notes:
This is a walkthrough of the implementation stages represented by the project. TypeScript types define the data. The UI then provides a way to create and inspect it. Zustand connects those actions to the 3D objects and camera. Recall logic updates retention status, while persistence keeps selected values after refresh. The project uses automated state tests, linting, type checks, formatting, and a production build. To run it locally, install Node.js 20.9 or newer, run npm ci, and start the development server.
Sources: README.md; package.json; tests/store.test.ts.

title: Quality, accessibility, and testing

columns.heading: Engineering checks
items: 19 automated store tests.
Validation of names, positions, and saved data.
Production build and lint checks passed.
Browser checks for custom rooms and persistence.

columns.heading: Usability support
items: Responsive navigation and forms.
Keyboard focus handling and Escape to close.
Reduced-motion and effects controls.
HTML study fallback when WebGL is unavailable.

foot: Functional checks do not establish learning outcomes or guarantee performance on every device.
notes:
The automated tests focus on state behavior, including rating rules, room changes, adding and editing anchors, persistence, and migration. Recent browser checks verified the custom-room form on desktop and mobile layouts. The browser used for those checks showed the HTML fallback, so those checks do not establish 3D performance on every graphics device. For a college demonstration, test the actual laptop and projector in advance. Educational effectiveness needs a separate student study.
Sources: tests/store.test.ts; prior successful test/build results; UI verification; README.md.

title: Limitations and next steps

columns.heading: Current limitations
items: Data stays on one browser and origin.
Ratings depend on honest self-assessment.
3D performance depends on the device.
No automatic revision schedule or class dashboard.

columns.heading: Future development
items: Accounts, cloud storage, and restore/import.
Spaced revision and fuller review history.
Lecturer templates and permission-based sharing.
A classroom study with delayed recall testing.

foot: Future work should preserve the simple study flow and the accessible fallback.
notes:
We should describe both the value and the limits honestly. The current version offers an individual study experience. It has no cloud backup, and a mastery label is a student's own assessment. A future system could add scheduled revision, account-based access, and lecturer-created material. Before claiming a learning advantage, we would compare groups using the same content and study time, then measure recall after a delay. That would test the learning experience rather than only the software.
Sources: README.md; proposed roadmap and evaluation design.

title: Live demonstration
steps: Open Computer Science
Select an anchor and explain its connection to a place.
Create Mathematics
Choose a name, icon, and color for a new palace.
Add one memory
Enter a short note and assign an artifact.
Run a recall attempt
Hide the title, attempt the answer, reveal, and rate.
Refresh the page
Show that the palace, note, and progress remain.
foot: Use demonstration notes. If 3D is unavailable, continue through the anchor list.
notes:
This demonstration takes about three minutes. Introduce one existing anchor first, then create a new subject only if there is no palace with that name already. Add a short concept such as the Pythagorean theorem, with its condition that the triangle is right-angled. Use Recall Challenge to demonstrate an answer attempt followed by reveal and rating. Refresh to show local saving. If the room fails to render, the HTML list still demonstrates the study workflow. Avoid deleting or changing another person's notes.
Source: implemented workflow and fallback in README.md.

title: NeuroQuest's purpose
lead: NeuroQuest turns subject notes into spatial memory cues and gives students a structured way to practise remembering.
notes:
To conclude, the purpose of NeuroQuest is to help students connect information with places and practise retrieval in a personal study environment. Our project combines a responsive frontend, interactive 3D graphics, and local persistence. The next stage is to test the experience with learners and, if useful, add a secure backend for synchronization and teaching workflows. Thank you. We welcome questions about the learning idea, how the website works, and what we would improve next.
Source: project implementation and proposed roadmap.
